prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

You work with what you are given, the red clay of grief, the black clay of stubbornness going on after. Clay that tastes of care or carelessness, clay that smells of the bottoms of rivers or dust. Each thought is a life you have lived or failed to live, each word is a dish you have eaten or left on the table. There are honeys so bitter no one would willingly choose to take them. The clay takes them: honey of weariness, honey of vanity, honey of cruelty, fear. This rebus—slip and stubbornness, bottom of river, my own consumed life— when will I learn to read it plainly, slowly, uncolored by hope or desire? Not to understand it, only to see. As water given sugar sweetens, given salt grows salty, we become our choices. Each yes, each no continues, this one a ladder, that one an anvil or cup. The ladder leans into its darkness. The anvil leans into its silence. The cup sits empty. How can I enter this question the clay has asked?

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: You, Clay, Each

outputs.L1:
You work with what you are given: the red clay of grief, the black clay of the stubbornness that carries on afterward. Clay that tastes of care or carelessness; clay that smells of river bottoms or dust. Each thought is a life you have lived or failed to live; each word, a dish you have eaten or left on the table.

Some honeys are so bitter that no one would willingly choose to taste them. The clay accepts them: the honey of weariness, the honey of vanity, the honey of cruelty, of fear. This rebus—slip and stubbornness, river bottom, my own consumed life—when will I learn to read it plainly, slowly, uncolored by hope or desire? Not to understand it, only to see.

As water sweetens when given sugar and grows salty when given salt, so we become our choices. Each yes, each no, continues: this one a ladder, that one an anvil or a cup. The ladder leans into its darkness. The anvil leans into its silence. The cup sits empty.

How can I enter the question the clay has asked?
outputs.L2:
You shape whatever lies before you: grief’s rust-colored earth and the dark soil of persistence that follows loss. It carries the flavor of tenderness or neglect, and the scent of riverbeds or dry dust. Every thought contains a life embraced or abandoned; every word resembles food consumed or allowed to remain untouched. Some sweetness is so harsh that no one would accept it by choice. Yet the earth absorbs everything—the nectar of exhaustion, pride, cruelty, and fear.

When will I decipher this riddle of yielding and endurance, of river floor and the life I have used up—clearly, patiently, without hope or longing tinting what I see? I do not seek comprehension, only honest sight. Water becomes sweet with sugar and briny with salt; in the same way, our decisions form us. Every acceptance and refusal carries forward: one becomes a ladder, another an anvil, another a cup. The ladder angles toward darkness. The anvil inclines toward quiet. The cup remains vacant. How am I to step inside the question posed by this earth?
outputs.L3:
Life asks us to work with difficult and often contradictory materials: grief and stubbornness, care and carelessness. These forces are woven into ordinary experience, shaping how we respond to loss, responsibility, conflict, and change. We do not encounter them as abstract ideas, but as realities that influence our relationships, decisions, and understanding of ourselves.

Every thought we form and every word we speak bears the imprint of a life lived—or of a life neglected, accepted, or abandoned. Language carries traces of our choices and omissions, revealing not only what we value but also what we have refused to confront. Even silence can reflect what has been left behind.

Human experience also absorbs bitterness. Weariness, vanity, cruelty, and fear become part of our inner world, sometimes quietly and gradually. To perceive life truthfully, we must recognize these emotions without letting hope or desire disguise them. Clear perception does not require abandoning hope; it means refusing to let hope replace reality.

Within this uncertain landscape, our choices continually shape the people we become. We may never fully understand their ultimate meaning or consequences, but each act of care, avoidance, courage, or surrender contributes to the pattern of a life. Meaning may remain unresolved, yet responsibility endures: we are formed, day by day, by how we engage with what life gives us.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents self-examination as a difficult, physical process. Rather than treating grief and regret as abstract emotions, the speaker gives them tangible forms through images of clay, honey, water, and familiar household objects. These materials carry different associations: clay can be molded but also hardened; honey suggests sweetness, preservation, and stickiness; water cleanses and sustains while remaining impossible to hold; and ordinary objects accumulate the traces of daily life. Together, they create a world in which memory and identity are embedded in matter.

Through these metaphors, the speaker confronts not only what has happened but also what might have happened. Lived choices have consequences that gather over time, while unlived possibilities exert their own pressure through absence and regret. Grief therefore becomes more than mourning a single loss. It includes sorrow for abandoned paths, missed opportunities, and versions of the self that could never be realized. Yet the poem also emphasizes persistence: despite this weight, the speaker continues to examine, endure, and reshape experience.

Clay becomes especially significant as an image of human identity. A person may seem solid and complete, but the poem suggests that the self is continually formed by action. Every decision leaves an impression, just as pressure leaves a mark on clay. Some choices reshape a life dramatically, while others alter it almost imperceptibly. Even refusing to choose becomes part of this shaping process. Identity is therefore not fixed; it is the accumulated result of countless moments of decision, acceptance, avoidance, and loss.

The poem ultimately insists on the necessity of clear sight. Hope and desire may offer comfort, but they can also distort reality by making people see the life they wanted rather than the life they actually made. Genuine self-knowledge requires looking without such illusions, acknowledging both what has been chosen and what has been surrendered. This recognition is painful because it offers no easy consolation. Nevertheless, the poem presents it as essential: people are continually shaped by their choices, and living honestly means accepting the form those choices have given them.
outputs.L5: You are made of clay, shaped by every touch of joy, sorrow, and time. Each experience leaves an imprint, yet you remain unfinished—always able to soften, change, and become something new.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about grief, resilience, and how our choices shape who we become, using clay, honey, water, a ladder, an anvil, and an empty cup as recurring images.
counterfactuals.output:
Grief came first as water, finding every seam in the house of me. It filled the empty cup beside my bed, climbed the walls in moonlit silence, loosened the clay of my name until I could no longer tell what had been shaped by love and what by loss.

I carried that cup everywhere.

Some mornings, sorrow tasted like iron from the anvil. Some evenings, like honey darkened in the jar—sweet because I had loved, bitter because love had nowhere left to go. I learned that memory does not ask permission. It drips. It floods. It hardens. It waits.

There was a ladder leaning against the sky, though no one could promise where it led. Each rung was a choice: rise, remain; open, close; forgive, refuse. My hands blistered around the wood. Below me, the old life lay broken into pieces of clay. Above me, clouds gathered their water.

Still, I climbed.

Resilience was not a trumpet. It was the quiet anvil beneath each day, receiving blow after blow and keeping its dark, steady shape. It was my hands returning to the clay, though they trembled. It was pouring water into what had cracked, pressing the edges together, beginning again without pretending the vessel had never been broken.

And sometimes resilience was honey: one gold thread offered to the empty cup. A friend at the door. Bread warming in the oven. Sunlight laid across the floorboards. The sudden mercy of laughter, startling as a bird.

I began to understand that we are not only what happens to us. We are also what we lift to the anvil, what we soften with water, what we sweeten with honey. We are the ladder we choose to climb and the rung we offer to someone below. We are clay, yes—marked by every hand, every fall—but also the hands that shape.

Years passed. The cup remained empty in one sense: no one returned. Yet emptiness changed its voice. It became room. It became breath. It became a small, round sky I could hold without drowning.

Now, when grief comes as water, I do not bar the door. I set the cup between us. I let it fill. Then I carry it to the clay and begin.

The anvil waits. The honey shines. The ladder leans into morning.

And choice by choice, wound by wound, I become someone who can climb while carrying water—someone who can be broken and still make a vessel, someone who has tasted absence and yet leaves sweetness on the rim.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a contemplative passage in the style of a modern meditative poet, exploring the difficulty of seeing one’s life clearly without hope or desire distorting it.
counterfactuals.output:
To look at a life without asking it  
to become another life—

this may be the hardest kind of seeing.

Hope leans over the glass,  
breathing its small weather onto everything.  
Desire places a candle behind each face  
and calls the glow truth.

Meanwhile, the day stands quietly where it is:  
a cup cooling on the table,  
a door we did not open,  
the body carrying its old, unanswerable music.

Can we meet these things without bargaining?  
Can we let the past be neither wound nor lesson,  
but simply the country we have crossed?

For one clear moment, perhaps,  
the mind stops polishing the horizon.  
Nothing is promised. Nothing is taken away.

And there—beneath what we wanted,  
beneath what we feared would never come—  
our life waits, plain and luminous,  
not asking to be loved,  
only seen.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an original prose poem that begins with “You work with what you are given” and ends with a question about clay. Make the language tactile, philosophical, and emotionally restrained.
counterfactuals.output: You work with what you are given: a table scarred by knives, a cup cooling between your hands, the body’s small republic of salt and ache. You learn pressure before permission—the thumb’s slow argument, the palm translating weight into form. Nothing becomes whole; it only agrees, briefly, to hold together. Even grief can be turned without spectacle, dampened, centered, made useful enough to carry water. Still, each vessel keeps the memory of collapse, the soft inward fold beneath the glaze. We call this endurance, though perhaps it is only matter accepting touch. And when the hands are gone, what will the silence ask of the clay?
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, image-rich meditation on regret and self-knowledge in which thoughts are unlived lives, words are unfinished meals, and every yes or no becomes a physical object.
counterfactuals.output:
At night, my thoughts climb down from the attic wearing the clothes of people I did not become.

One is a beekeeper. He carries summer inside his sleeves. One is a woman who took the train west and now sleeps beside an ocean that combs blue fire through her hair. One has a child. One has none. One learned to forgive early and walks without the limp I have mistaken for my name.

They gather around my bed, these unlived lives, smelling of rain, engine oil, milk, foreign airports. They do not accuse me. That would be easier. They unpack their small, impossible belongings: a wedding ring warm from another hand, a key to a house never built, a passport stamped by countries that exist only when I close my eyes.

I ask them what they want.

They open their mouths, and my old words fall out.

Every word is an unfinished meal.

I find *sorry* cooling in a bowl, its skin gone gray. *Stay* is a pear with one bite taken from it, browning on the windowsill. *I love you* lies under a silver lid, untouched, while flies circle the chandelier. There are sentences I began twenty years ago still waiting at the table, candles burned down to their sockets, napkins stiff with dust.

I have been hungry all my life, yet I leave everything uneaten.

In the cellar, my yeses and noes have become physical things.

The yeses are small brass animals. They twitch in drawers, bright with handling. Some have wings soldered to their backs; some have teeth. The yes I gave from fear is a gold mouse trapped beneath a glass. The yes I meant is a bell, green with weather, that rings whenever someone speaks my true name.

The noes are heavier. Black stones. Iron doors. A row of anchors hanging from hooks. One no is a knife I sharpened for years and never used. Another is a wall with my mother’s shadow still moving across it. The smallest no is lodged behind my heart. Doctors have seen it on their instruments: a white seed, a cold star, the fossil of a mouth refusing to open.

I once believed regret was a road leading backward. Now I know it is a room that rearranges itself while you sleep. The window becomes a mirror. The mirror becomes a door. You step through expecting the past and find only yourself, older, carrying the same lamp.

Its light is not kind, but it is exact.

Under it, I see that some doors were never locked. I see the fingerprints on the key. I see how often I called my fear wisdom, how elegantly I dressed my silence, how I placed a crown on hesitation and knelt before it.

Self-knowledge arrives not as a revelation but as an animal returning from the woods. Mud-footed. Starving. Wary of the hand. It stands at the edge of the firelight and resembles me so closely I begin to weep.

The unlived lives sit beside me until dawn. The beekeeper hums. The woman from the western train closes her ocean-colored eyes. The child who was never born draws a house in the dust, then erases it with her sleeve.

“What should I have done?” I ask.

But they are already fading into the furniture, into the pale arithmetic of morning.

On the table, breakfast waits.

A plate of unfinished words. A cup filled with dark, steaming silence. Beside them lie today’s yes and today’s no: one a red fruit, the other a stone.

For once, I do not ask which is heavier.

I pick up each in turn. I feel its shape. I learn the temperature of my own hand.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you produce a short literary monologue about grief and moral choice, centered on red and black clay, bitter honey, riverbeds, and the idea that we become our decisions?
counterfactuals.output:
I was shaped from red clay, my brother from black—or so our mother used to say when she found us fighting by the riverbed. Red remembers blood, black remembers fire. Both stain the hands.

When he died, they brought me bitter honey in a cracked bowl. “Eat,” they said. “Grief must be given a sweetness, or it will devour you.” But the honey tasted of smoke, and I knew sweetness could lie.

The man who killed him knelt before me where the river had gone dry. Between us, the empty bed curled through the earth like a scar. I held the stone. I heard every old voice demanding balance: blood for blood, darkness for darkness.

Then I opened my hand.

Do not call it mercy. Mercy is clean, and nothing that day was clean. I spared him because I understood, at last, that we are not merely shaped once, like figures pressed from clay. We shape ourselves again with every choice. The hand closes, and we become the blow. The hand opens, and we become the loss we are willing to carry.

Rain came months later. The river returned, red at first, then black beneath the moon, bearing everything away except what I had chosen.

That remained.

That became me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
